title: Predicting Positive and Negative Links in Online Social Networks
coverage: Full text read in chunks, all 1624 lines of the text file (about 70k chars): front matter, abstract, introduction, Sec 2 data, Sec 3 sign prediction (features, logistic regression, balance and status reductions, cross-dataset transfer, heuristics), Sec 4 global structure, Sec 5 positive-edge existence, conclusion and references. Figures 1-3 are plot images, so only their captions and the prose were available; numbers are taken from the prose and tables. Annotations: the item lists n_annots 0 and an empty annot_sha12s, so no _annots file was read and paul_markup is empty; p.note is not set. Metadata hints corrected: authors expanded to full names; title, year 2010 and WWW 2010 venue confirmed in text; DOI does not appear in the text and is carried over from the item record. Page numbers come from the running page footers.
research_question: Can the sign (positive or negative) of a hidden directed link in an online social network be predicted from the signs of the rest of the network? Which local structural principles drive signed-link formation, and do they agree with balance and status theory? Secondary: does knowing negative links help predict positive links, and does global balance (factions) or global status (ordering) appear in these networks?
theory: Structural balance (Heider; Cartwright and Harary: the enemy of my friend is my enemy, and related triad rules), Davis's weak balance (makes no prediction on the enemy-of-enemy triad), and status theory (a positive edge means the source regards the target as higher status; a negative edge means lower; signs flip when direction flips). Each theory is written as a mapping from triad types to predicted sign and compared to learned logistic regression coefficients.
data: Three explicitly signed directed networks. Epinions trust/distrust: 119,217 nodes, 841,200 edges in Table 1 (text says 841,000), 85.0 percent positive, data from 1999 to 12 Aug 2003. Slashdot friend/foe: 82,144 nodes, 549,202 edges, 77.4 percent positive, crawled Feb 2009. Wikipedia admin-election votes: 7,118 users, 103,747 votes across 2,794 elections (1,235 promotions, 1,559 failures), 78.7 percent positive, from the Jan 2008 dump. Unit of analysis: a directed signed edge (u,v). Main accuracy results use edges with minimum embeddedness 25 (default Em), averaged over 10-fold cross validation, on a balanced sample in which each negative edge is paired with a random positive edge. Full unbalanced data is also reported.
method: Logistic regression over 23 features: 7 degree features (signed in- and out-degrees of u and v, total out-degree of u, total in-degree of v, and embeddedness C(u,v)) plus a 16-dimensional count of directed signed triad types formed by a common neighbor w with u and v. Reduced models: 4-type undirected balance counts, 4-type status counts after canonicalizing signs and directions, and 4-type counts on the all-positive subgraph. Hand-written heuristics (balance majority, status score sigma(x) with predicted sign from sigma(u) versus sigma(v), out-degree majority, in-degree majority) as baselines. Global tests: randomized local search for a two-set partition maximizing satisfied edges (balance), and random pairwise-swap search for a node ordering maximizing satisfied edges (status, as a maximum acyclic subgraph problem), compared with permuted-sign and degree-preserving rewired baselines. Positive-edge existence task: classifier separates true positive edges from matched non-edge pairs with equal embeddedness.
identification: No causal identification. Sign prediction is a leave-one-out style task: hide one edge sign and predict it from all other edges, reported with 10-fold cross validation. Cross-dataset transfer trains on one network and tests on another (Tables 6-7). Interpretation of triad coefficients as support for balance or status is associational.
scope: Three online platforms: a product-review trust site (Epinions), a technology news site with friend/foe tags (Slashdot), and Wikipedia adminship votes. Snapshots from roughly 2003 to 2009; web-era pre-2010 data. Population is active users with signed links. The paper's claims of generalization are limited to these three domains.

key_findings.finding: Learned logistic regression predicts edge signs with high accuracy on Epinions, beating the best error reported by Guha et al.
key_findings.numbers: Error on Epinions: 6.58 percent All23, 6.64 percent 16Triads, 11.45 percent Degree, versus 14.7 percent best in Guha et al. (balanced sample, Em 25)

key_findings.finding: On the full unbalanced data, random guessing is about 80 percent accurate and the logistic models reach 90-95 percent, roughly 15 points above chance; AUC is consistent with accuracy.
key_findings.numbers: Balanced sample: AUC about 0.90. Full data: AUC about 0.95; random accuracy about 0.80 on full data, 0.50 on balanced

key_findings.finding: Triad features gain value as embeddedness rises; degree features are stronger for edges with few common neighbors. Wikipedia accuracy is clearly lower than the other two networks even at high embeddedness.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative from Figure 1; accuracy curves plotted for Em = 0, 10, 25 with no table values in the text

key_findings.finding: The All23 model transfers across networks with little loss: even a model trained on Wikipedia predicts Epinions and Slashdot nearly as well as one trained on the target network.
key_findings.numbers: Test on Epinions: 0.9342 self-trained, 0.9249 trained on Slashdot, 0.9272 trained on Wikipedia. Test on Wikipedia: 0.8021 self-trained, 0.7722 trained on Epinions, 0.7717 trained on Slashdot

key_findings.finding: Balance theory matches the learned undirected triad coefficients for every triad type except enemy-of-enemy (mm), where the learned sign agrees with Davis's weak balance (no prediction) rather than balance.
key_findings.numbers: Undirected model coefficients listed per dataset (e.g., mm type disagrees across Epinions, Slashdot, Wikipedia); weak balance is the Davis 1963 variant

key_findings.finding: Balance-based models transfer well across domains, while learned status models transfer poorly and often do worse than untrained status baselines.
key_findings.numbers: BalanceLrn cross-dataset accuracies 0.90-0.92 among Epinions and Slashdot (e.g., 0.9027, 0.9166, 0.9020, 0.9203) versus BalanceDet 0.77-0.84; StatusLrn cross-dataset accuracies range about 0.61-0.83

key_findings.finding: A triad with v linking positively to w and w linking positively to u is evidence for a negative (u,v) edge in all three datasets, a pattern status theory explains as a lower-status reversal.
key_findings.numbers: Coefficient on the BB positive-path feature: -0.0692 Epinions, -0.0293 Slashdot, -0.0259 Wikipedia (all-positive subgraph model)

key_findings.finding: Simple heuristics beat chance but trail the learned models; out-degree of the edge generator is the strongest single cue on two of three networks, while in-degree performs poorly.
key_findings.numbers: Figure 3 curves only; no table values in the text. The text says out-degree (OutSign) performs well on two of three networks

key_findings.finding: A global status ordering fits the networks far better than chance or baselines: about 79 to 85 percent of edges respect an ordering, versus 50 percent for random orderings.
key_findings.numbers: Status satisfied fraction, Epinions/Slashdot/Wikipedia: network 0.7905/0.8221/0.8538; permuted signs 0.7241/0.7568/0.7767; rewired 0.6377/0.6644/0.6321

key_findings.finding: No significant global balance (faction) structure: partition objective values are essentially the positive fraction, and rewired networks with the same degrees score higher.
key_findings.numbers: Balance satisfied fraction, Epinions/Slashdot/Wikipedia: network 0.8344/0.8105/0.7809; permuted 0.8562/0.7779/0.7866; rewired 0.8993/0.8310/0.8316; trivial all-positive partition yields about 0.80

key_findings.finding: Negative links help predict where positive links exist: adding signed triad features beats positive-only features on all three networks.
key_findings.numbers: Positive-only accuracy 0.5612 Epinions, 0.5579 Slashdot, 0.6983 Wikipedia; positive plus negative accuracy 0.5911, 0.5953, 0.7114 (random 0.50)

limitations: Wikipedia sign prediction is much harder than the other two networks; the authors conjecture that public, consequential, information-based votes resist structural prediction.

Global balance and status searches are approximate heuristics; the status problem (maximum acyclic subgraph) is hard to approximate in the worst case, and the authors say local-to-global scaling of sign patterns remains an open question.
The naive all-positive partition already satisfies about 80 percent of edges, so balance objective values are only meaningful against rewired and permuted baselines.
Triad features carry little information at low embeddedness, and their performance drops again at very high embeddedness, reflecting a tradeoff in sparsity.
Balance and status each hold only approximately at the granularity where they are formulated; the 16-type model captures effects beyond either theory's resolution.
Learned status properties are more dataset-specific than balance properties, so the status model does not generalize as well.
Analysis is restricted to directed links; the undirected extension is mentioned but not developed. Opposite-direction edge pairs are treated as having no sign.
Edge count for Epinions is given as 841,000 in the text and 841,200 in Table 1.
measures: AUC on balanced and full samples
Degree features: signed in-/out-degree of u and v, embeddedness C(u,v)
16 signed directed triad counts; 4-type undirected balance and 4-type status counts
Logistic regression coefficients per triad type
Global satisfied-edge fraction for balance partitions and status orderings

short_quotes.quote: We find that the signs of links in the underlying social networks can be predicted with high accuracy
balance theory is in notably better alignment with the learned model for Epinions and Slashdot than it is for Wikipedia
we find no significant evidence for the kind of partitioning into factions that balance theory suggests at a global level
